A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

#9844. Jensen Huang's Nvidia Exit Is a Wake-Up Call for Startup Founders

This morning, November 12, 2026, Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang had resigned as President, CEO, and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair, which tells you it had been a one-man show for 33 years.

The board's word is "resigned." Most headlines went with "ousted." Days earlier, CBS had reported the board was preparing to remove him. You decide which word fits.

Here's the short version. A New York Times report alleged multiple affairs, including one with a Singapore data-center executive whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, at a firm that bought billions of dollars of Nvidia hardware. Another alleged affair was with a senior executive who reported directly to him. Huang had already admitted infidelity in a memo to employees on November 9. Then came national-security questions, demands from lawmakers, and a stock that fell roughly 10%, wiping out hundreds of billions in market value. After that, the end came quickly.

Set the morality aside for a minute, because the board didn't need to settle it. What I want founders to notice is the mechanics.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in a Denny's in 1993. He bet the company on GPUs, then on CUDA, then on AI, and grew it into a company worth more than $4 trillion. He is about as close to a founder-god as Silicon Valley has.

And he had no structural protection whatsoever.

Nvidia has a single class of stock: one share, one vote. Its board was made up of independent directors plus Jensen, and it could remove the CEO with or without cause by simple majority. Mark Zuckerberg can't be fired. Larry Page couldn't be fired. Jensen Huang, the man who made the AI age possible, could be shown the door in a week.

If that doesn't make every founder reading this check their charter, nothing will.

Founders don't usually lose control in one dramatic boardroom scene. They lose it gradually, through a series of small and individually reasonable decisions.

Act I: One share, one vote. For about sixty years the NYSE refused to list companies with dual-class shares. The idea was that voting power should track economic risk. Ford's 1956 IPO, where the family kept super-voting shares, was the famous exception. Media dynasties like the New York Times Company got a pass on the grounds of editorial independence.

Act II: Google changes the rules. In 2004, Larry Page and Sergey Brin took Google public with Class B shares carrying 10 votes each. The public bought it anyway. Facebook, LinkedIn, Snap, and Alibaba all followed. Hong Kong held out, lost Alibaba's $25 billion IPO to New York, and changed its rules in 2018. By 2021–22, about 47% of U.S. tech IPOs were dual-class.

Act III: the slow loss of your majority. This is the part nobody puts in the pitch deck. According to Carta's 2025–26 data, founders typically hold:

Capital intensity makes it worse. If your company works with atoms (chips, robots, biotech), you burn two to three times the cash of a SaaS company and sell more of the company at every round. Jensen is the hardware founder's cautionary tale: decades of capital-hungry growth, and nothing left to vote with when it counted.

The lesson: you don't lose control when the board votes. You lose it, one term sheet at a time, years before.

Every founder knows this story, and every founder assumes it couldn't happen to them.

In 1985, Steve Jobs was 30, a co-founder of Apple, and the person most responsible for its products and culture. He had no super-voting shares. The Macintosh launched to great reviews and disappointing sales. Jobs's "my way or the highway" style wore everyone out. John Sculley, the Pepsi executive Jobs had personally recruited with the famous "sugar water" pitch, moved to take away his operating authority.

Jobs tried to get Sculley removed instead. The plan leaked, the board backed Sculley, and Jobs, with no structural power at all, resigned and went off to start NeXT.

What followed was a twelve-year slide that brought Apple to within about 90 days of insolvency in 1997. The board, out of options, bought NeXT, mostly to get Jobs back. You know the rest: iMac, iPod, iPhone, and the most valuable company on Earth.

Dual-class advocates like to say that if Jobs had held super-voting stock, Apple would have skipped a lost decade.

Maybe. I'll give you the more uncomfortable version. The Jobs who got fired was probably not the Jobs who saved Apple. NeXT and Pixar humbled him and taught him things, and he came back a better CEO. Getting fired may have been the most valuable thing that ever happened to him, though it's hard to see it that way while it's happening.

Adam Neumann got the thing Jobs never had: 20 votes per share. The board couldn't fire him, investors couldn't overrule him, and he ran the company accordingly.

When the S-1 came out in August 2019, public investors saw $47 billion in lease obligations against $4 billion in committed revenue, plus governance that made Apple's 1985 board look like the Federalist Papers. The IPO collapsed and SoftBank had to fund a bailout. Neumann was out, and in 2023 the company filed for Chapter 11.

Here's the lesson I care about most. Super-voting stock does two things: it protects you from the market's panic, and it protects you from your own mistakes. The first is valuable. The second can kill the company. The same structure that would have saved 1985 Jobs from Sculley also saved Neumann from anyone who might have told him no.

So what should you actually do? Here is the playbook, roughly by stage. If you can, negotiate these terms when you have leverage, which means before you need the money.

The academics have a useful framework for this. Agency costs are the damage a founder does when nobody can stop them; that's WeWork. Principal costs are the damage investors do when they're in charge: panic, short-termism, and a buyback where an R&D budget should be. That's 1985 Apple.

Law professors Zohar Goshen and Richard Squire argue the right structure minimizes the sum of the two. A visionary founder in a 20-year bet like AI, VR, or rockets should get more insulation. A mature company with a founder who has drifted should get less.

The data supports this. Dual-class firms trade at a premium at IPO, because markets value the founder's vision. Around seven to ten years later, that premium tends to become a discount as the founder's economic stake shrinks while their votes don't.

So the goal isn't maximum control. It's control that fits where your company is in its life: enough insulation to make long-term bets, with a working mechanism for someone to say "stop" if you lose your way.

Jensen had plenty of the first and none of the second, which was fine for 33 years until this week. Neumann had too much of both. Jobs had none, and it took a lost decade to fix.

Here's what I expect over the next five years.

1. The Jensen effect on fundraising. Founders raising in 2027 will bring up Nvidia in every board-composition negotiation, and investors will bring up WeWork. Both are fair points.

2. Trust-based structures as the new middle ground. Anthropic's S-1 shows a new model. The founders hold a Class F share that gives them 50.1% of ordinary votes, while an independent Long-Term Benefit Trust with no economic stake elects a majority of the board. The founders control the shareholder vote, and the trust controls the board. OpenAI's foundation keeps exclusive power over its PBC's board even though Microsoft owns 27% of the equity. These are deliberate checks and balances in a company charter, and you'll see others copy them.

3. Sunsets become standard. Perpetual founder control is ending. Index providers, proxy advisors, and institutional investors all agree on that. Expect seven-to-ten-year sunsets to become the price of a dual-class IPO.

4. The jurisdiction wars continue. Delaware vs. Texas vs. Nevada. Your state of incorporation is now a strategic decision, not a box your lawyer checks.

5. Character as a governance mechanism. This is the uncomfortable one. As founders gain more structural protection, the remaining risks come from conduct: personal behavior, conflicts of interest, national security. Those risks don't care how many votes your shares carry.

My closing advice to every engineer-founder reading this:

Fight for control early, when it's cheap. Protect it with structure, not just goodwill. Give it an expiration date before someone else does. And above all, build a company and a character that a board would never want to fire.

Jensen Huang built one of the greatest companies in history and still lost it in a week. Your share structure can't fully protect you from yourself, so you'll have to manage that part on your own.

#9843. Lessons from the November 2026 Microsoft 365 Outage: Designing Resilient OneDrive Transfers

Incident handling, Microsoft Graph throttling, resumable jobs, and the limits of cloud-to-cloud backup during a provider outage.

On November 12–13, 2026, a major Microsoft 365 service disruption exposed a familiar dependency: applications built on a cloud platform are only as reachable as the platform's identity, metadata, and file APIs.

Microsoft tracked incidents under MO1550821 (broader Microsoft 365 connectivity) and EX1550543 (Exchange Online). Public notices in Japan documented trouble accessing OneDrive alongside other Microsoft 365 applications; Hitotsubashi University's notice is one example.

The incident's reported infrastructure symptoms included unexpectedly unavailable servers and increased load. Those are incident reports, not proof that every Microsoft Graph endpoint failed or that any particular HTTP status code was widespread. What follows is an engineering playbook for the kinds of failures cloud-transfer systems may encounter during an outage.

A transfer failure can have several causes. Classify them before retrying:

These are general diagnostic examples, not a list of confirmed errors from the November incident. Microsoft documents their Graph error semantics separately.

For Microsoft 365 tenants, first correlate error spikes with Service Health and incident notices. Record timestamps, endpoint, tenant or account scope, sanitized error code, and request ID. Avoid logging OAuth tokens or file contents.

A naive retry loop can turn a bad incident into a worse one. Microsoft Graph's throttling guidance says to use Retry-After when supplied for 429 responses; otherwise, an exponential-backoff strategy is recommended.

A simplified policy—not a production-ready library—might look like this:

Real systems also need a retry budget, request deadlines, cancellation, respect for HTTP-date-form Retry-After, and careful distinction between retry-safe reads and operations that create side effects. Do not blindly replay a non-idempotent upload or finalize request. SDKs may already retry some Graph requests automatically, so check for double retry layers.

For repeated copies, avoid enumerating the entire drive every time. Where applicable, Microsoft Graph delta queries can track changes and reduce unnecessary polling. Your implementation must still handle deleted items, invalidated state, permissions, pagination, and eventual consistency.

If a one-way mirror replicates accidental deletion, you have two copies of the same mistake. A recovery design should ask whether the destination is separately accessible, whether it retains versions, whether deletion propagation is appropriate, and whether restores have been tested.

When OneDrive itself is inaccessible, a new API-driven copy may be impossible. The best outage-time option is usually a second copy that already exists in another provider or an offline store.

Not every team needs to build and maintain its own migration worker. RiceDrive is a cloud-to-cloud transfer product that lets users connect OneDrive to destinations such as Google Drive, Dropbox, MEGA, Box, pCloud, and selected object stores—without a manual local download/upload cycle.

The product supports 40+ cloud platforms and protocols. Available workflows include background tasks, transfer logs, filters, and scheduled transfers; the free tier includes 10GB of monthly transfer traffic.

A useful first workflow is OneDrive → a separate destination account, using one-way copy settings, a limited test folder, and post-transfer verification. Work or school accounts may require administrative approval, and file-sharing links and version history should not be assumed to migrate unchanged.

See the illustrated OneDrive backup and transfer guide for setup steps and provider considerations.

This is a product-level backup option, not a claim that RiceDrive internally implements every architectural pattern in the diagram above. Nor can RiceDrive read OneDrive files through an unavailable Microsoft API. Set up and validate the independent copy while both providers are operating normally.

Bottom line: Availability incidents will happen. The engineering goal is to make a temporary upstream failure visible, recoverable, and less disruptive to users—not to pretend that another API client can repair an unavailable source.

References: Microsoft Service Health · Hitotsubashi University outage report · Microsoft Graph throttling · Microsoft Graph delta queries.

Disclosure: This article is published by the RiceDrive team. RiceDrive is mentioned as one option for cloud-to-cloud transfers.

#9842. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. #9841. Decision Models in Hugging Face

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​

∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

The model again produces a probability distribution:

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p)

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997

Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

#9840. WordPress or Custom Code? How to Choose for Your Business Website

Choosing between WordPress and custom code is one of the first decisions for any new business website in India. Neither option is "better" in general. The right answer depends on what the site has to do, who will maintain it, and how much it will change over time.

WordPress works well when your site is mostly content: a home page, service pages, a blog, a contact form. Reasons teams choose it:

The trade-off is maintenance. Core, theme and plugin updates need regular attention, and every extra plugin adds some security and performance risk. A lean setup with few, well-supported plugins usually performs far better than a heavily stacked one.

Custom development (for example a Node, Laravel or Django application with a hand-built front end) is worth considering when:

The trade-off is cost and speed. Every feature is built and tested by your team or agency, and changes to content may need a developer unless a CMS is built in.

Also consider a hybrid: WordPress as a headless CMS with a custom front end, or a custom application sitting next to a WordPress blog on a subdomain. These can work, but they add moving parts, so use them only when there is a clear reason.

If you are weighing the two options for a real project, it helps to talk to a team that builds both and can explain trade-offs in plain language. You can learn about the services of a web development firm in India such as MGTech Labs, or browse practical guides on the MGTech Labs blog before you make a call.

Whichever route you choose, write down your requirements first, ask for a clear scope, and plan for maintenance from day one. A well-maintained simple site beats a neglected complex one every time.

#9838. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.

#9834. Educational Byte: What Is a Liquidity Pool in Crypto —and Why It Matters

To understand this one, let’s first look at the "traditional" processes for exchanging money via digital platforms. We can commonly see two mechanisms: you exchange your currency directly against the exchange or provider’s own funds, or an order book is used. This order book records all buy and sell orders placed by users and provides liquidity based on that activity. The more orders in place, the more liquidity. Well, liquidity pools have come to replace these models in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols.

A liquidity pool in crypto is a supply of tokens locked inside a smart contract on a DeFi protocol. It has the purpose of offering liquidity to other users for swaps, loans, or any financial activity on that specific protocol. The locked funds come from other users who, in exchange for providing this liquidity to the pool, receive rewards in the form of transaction fees and even governance tokens.

This way, no powerful middlemen are required to safely access financial instruments. It’s the users themselves who provide liquidity in a decentralized environment.

Typically, a liquidity pool holds two tokens, such as GBYTE and USDC. Liquidity providers are the ones who deposit these token pairs—and they could be anyone with the available funds. Then, those funds help to create a big reserve that traders can use for their own operations, like swaps. The smart contract keeps track of those balances and applies the rules that govern each trade.

Price adjustment comes from the reserves themselves. In a classic Automated Market Maker (AMM) model, a simple formula is used: X × Y = K, where X and Y represent the quantities of the two tokens and K is the constant. When someone swaps, let’s say, USDC for GBYTE, the pool receives one asset and releases the other, changing the balances and thus the price for the next trade. Depending on the available liquidity, a larger trade may create more price impact, which implies that the price could drop by a certain percentage for the next swap.

For liquidity providers, the platform may give them LP tokens as proof of their share of the pool. These tokens can be used to track and redeem that share, including the depositor’s portion of trading fees earned by the pool. Their reward is directly proportional to their contribution to the pool.

Some pools may be rewarded with additional incentives. For instance, in the Obyte-based DEX Oswap.io, all liquidity providers to a few selected pools receive 100 GBYTE every seven days, distributed in proportion to their contributed liquidity. That’s an additional incentive on top of fees.

A healthy financial environment needs liquidity, and liquidity doesn’t come out of nowhere. For trades and other operations to actually happen, funds must be available, and someone must put the funds there. In traditional finance, that someone is often a powerful middleman, like a bank. But cryptocurrencies weren’t created to rely on powerful middlemen; they were created to get rid of them. So, we have liquidity pools instead.

By using this model, everyone can access liquidity without cumbersome requirements or censorship risks. Meanwhile, liquidity providers receive rewards for their contributions in what is, without a doubt, a type of investment that can yield a good and frequent passive return. Of course, the specific rules and the censorship resistance vary from network to network.

Obyteuses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) structure without miners or “validators,” which increases its decentralization and drastically reduces the mere possibility of censorship or blocking. In Oswap.io, each pool has its own parameters and governance, but all are decentralized and open for everyone to participate. That’s the whole idea; that’s why liquidity pools matter: they offer a freedom we can’t enjoy in traditional financial products.

#9833. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9832. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9831. I Played Three Mobile Games to Find the Math Hiding Inside Them

Games feel like pure fun, but every jump, camera swing and score counter is powered by math. For a class assignment I stopped playing like a player and started playing like a developer. I analysed three free mobile games: Subway Surfers and Vector from the recommended list, and Temple Run as my own pick. I looked for six ideas from class: distance, vectors, algebra, dot product, cross product and linear interpolation (lerp).

I can’t see the source code, so what follows is based on what I observed. Where I’m inferring how something works, I say “likely”.

I played each game for at least 30 minutes across 12 sessions, took screenshots and wrote notes as I went. You can also watch my video walkthrough: https://youtu.be/Mz7PZpl1Eoo

Quick facts: Mobile, endless runner, Kiloo and SYBO Games, 2012.

You play a graffiti artist running along train tracks, dodging trains and barriers while collecting coins. It is easy to learn (just swipe), speeds up gradually, and small missions keep giving you a reason to play one more run. My best run during testing scored 2,776, and a later run passed 6,000.

Distance: Score climbs as you travel forward, and coins are collected when you get close enough. A pickup check likely compares the gap between player and coin to a small radius: d = sqrt(dx^2 + dz^2) < r. Direction and vectors: The runner always has a forward velocity, plus sideways movement between three lanes. The forward speed grows over time, which is how the game gets harder. Algebra: The x2 multiplier, the coin counter and the mission bars (20/20 coins, 5/5 jumps) are all simple formulas. Score is roughly distance points times the multiplier, and mission progress is current / target. Dot product: Obstacles ahead matter and obstacles behind don’t. A check like forward . toObstacle > 0 would tell the game that something is in front of me. Cross product: Lane changes are left or right. The sign of the cross product of the forward direction and the direction to the target lane would tell the game which way to lean the character. Lerp: The runner glides between lanes instead of teleporting, and the camera follows smoothly.

When I swipe, the game likely sets a target lane, for example x = -1, 0 or +1 times the lane width. Every frame the runner moves a fraction of the way there:

x_new = x_current + (x_target - x_current) * t

That is lerp, and it is why the character glides. Jumping is probably simple physics: y(t) = v0*t - 0.5*g*t^2. Collision detection then compares the runner’s box with the boxes of trains and barriers. Since lanes are fixed, the game only has to check obstacles in the same lane, which keeps it fast on phones.

What works well: The controls are simple and responsive, the missions give clear short goals, and the bright colours make obstacles readable at high speed.

What I would improve: Fewer video-ad prompts on the mission screen, because they interrupt the flow. I would also add adaptive difficulty that adjusts obstacle patterns to how well the player has been doing, and a swipe sensitivity setting for different screen sizes.

Quick facts: Mobile, parkour platform runner, Nekki, 2012 . Vector is a 2D side-view parkour game. You control a silhouetted runner across rooftops, using a few on-screen buttons to jump, slide and vault. The art style and fluid animation are what make it enjoyable.

Distance: Bonus cubes (1/6 in the HUD) are collected when the runner reaches them, and the camera keeps the runner at a set distance on screen. Direction and vectors: In my screenshot the runner slides down a sloped roof, so the movement follows the slope, not a flat line. On a slope of angle theta the velocity is likely v = speed * (cos theta, -sin theta). Algebra: Collectible counters (cubes, objectives, coins), star ratings and unlock costs like 600 coins are numbers that increase or are compared to thresholds. Dot product: A dot product between the runner’s facing direction and the direction to an obstacle shows whether it is ahead, which could trigger a vault or slide. Cross product: The runner’s body tilts to match the roof. Aligning a character to a surface needs the surface normal, which comes from a cross product in 3D or a perpendicular in 2D. Lerp: Running, sliding and jumping blend into each other instead of snapping between poses, and the menu panels slide in smoothly.

One mechanic explained: sliding down a slope

The game needs the direction of the surface, the tangent vector t = (cos theta, -sin theta). Gravity pulls straight down, but only the part along the slope speeds the runner up. A dot product finds that part:

A steeper slope means a bigger sin theta, so the runner accelerates faster. The body is rotated to match the roof angle, and when the roof ends, the speed is kept and the runner enters a jump arc. That is why timing your tricks matters.

What works well: The silhouette against a detailed background keeps the runner easy to see, two buttons trigger many context-sensitive moves, and the cube and bonus goals encourage replaying levels.

What I would improve: A shorter step-by-step tutorial, because the Lab text covered a large part of the menu with many pop-ups. I would also add a ghost replay of my best run so I can learn better lines, and a small trajectory hint when jumping off a slope.

Quick facts: Mobile, 3D endless runner, Imangi Studios, 2011.

An explorer steals a cursed idol and is chased through temple ruins by demon monkeys. I chose it because it is free, it runs on mobile, and it clearly uses 3D vectors, a chase camera and pursuit. The monsters are always visible behind you, which keeps the tension constant.

Distance: Score grows with distance run (260 at the start of one run, 42,070 later). The gap between me and the monsters works like a danger value that likely shrinks after a stumble, and coins are picked up with a distance check. Direction and vectors: The player runs forward and turns 90 degrees at corners. Position updates each frame by velocity * time, and tilting the phone adds a sideways component. Algebra: Score, coins (0, then 279) and the achievement count (57) are running totals compared against thresholds. Dot product: Coins and obstacles ahead are relevant while the monsters are behind. A dot product between the forward vector and the vector to an object decides front or back. Cross product: At a corner the game must know if my swipe turns left or right and rotate the camera the same way. The sign of the cross product gives that direction. Lerp: Turns look smooth, the camera swings behind the player after each corner, and coins spin.

The camera sits behind and above the player. Each frame its target is:

camera_target = player_pos - forward * d + up * h

It doesn’t snap there. It moves toward it with lerp:

camera_pos = camera_pos + (camera_target - camera_pos) * t

When I turn at a corner, the forward vector rotates by 90 degrees and the camera swings round smoothly. This is what gives the long stone bridge such a strong sense of depth and speed.

What works well: The monsters behind you create real urgency, the swipe and tilt controls are intuitive, and the camera sells the speed.

What I would improve: Modernise the textures and character models, add daily challenges such as “collect 100 coins without jumping” for variety, and add a subtle screen-edge effect that grows as the monsters get closer so the chase distance is easier to read.

Lerp and algebra showed up the most across the three games. Lerp is behind the smooth lane changes in Subway Surfers, the animation blending in Vector and the camera swing in Temple Run, so almost every smooth motion on screen seems to use it. Algebra is in every score, multiplier, coin counter and mission bar. Distance was a close third, because pickups, chasers and obstacles all depend on how far apart things are.

Before this assignment I only noticed whether a game was fun. Now I notice why the camera lags slightly, why a character glides instead of jumping between positions, and how a simple multiplier shapes what I do next. Vectors and distance control movement and detection, dot and cross products handle direction, algebra drives scores and rewards, and lerp makes everything feel smooth. The best designs make that math invisible, and I can now imagine building these mechanics myself.

Watch my video walkthrough: https://youtu.be/Mz7PZpl1Eoo Screenshots from all three games: https://imgur.com/a/8Bx9eOZ

#9830. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9829. How our Pipeline orchestrates LBO Due Diligence ?

Welcome to the third chapter of our four-part series, **Building Sovereign, Hallucination-Free Financial AI. In Part 1: Building a Deterministic Financial Agent with Dual-Persona LoRA, we prohibited probabilistic language models from performing arithmetic. In Part 2: How our Training Recipe led us to "Hallucination", we stepped into the machine room: fine-tuning an 8B model.

Today, we address the ultimate frontier: What happens when the financial question cannot fit into a single prompt or table? How do we orchestrate complex, multi-step workflows like a Cross-Table LBO Due Diligence across disparate financial statements—and how do we ensure the final synthesis sent to the boardroom is 100% immune to semantic inversion and hallucination?

In Part 2, we showed that when an 8B specialist model encounters missing variables in a messy financial filing, standard RLHF conditions it to panic: it grabs loosely related numbers from adjacent rows to satisfy the prompt, falling directly into the Compensation Hallucination Trap.

We fixed this at the micro-level with response-only masking and rejection circuit breakers. But in enterprise finance, you quickly encounter a macro-level barrier:

Imagine handing an autonomous agent an audited annual report (like the official French standalone filing — comptes sociaux — of Renault SAS, Renault Group's main operating subsidiary) and asking:

"Is a leveraged buyout (LBO) of this target financially feasible based on its latest audited accounts?"

Answering this is not a one-shot retrieval problem. It requires navigating across multiple disparate accounting schedules:

If you shove all these tables into a single context window and ask an 8B model to reason through all five steps at once, attention anxiety returns with a vengeance. The model conflates standalone operating subsidiary debt with consolidated group figures, divides equity by operating profit, or produces subtle, catastrophic semantic inversions.

To solve this, we must enforce Separation of Concerns at the system architecture level.

Instead of burdening a single specialist model with planning, document navigation, tool invocation, and narrative synthesis, we architected a Bilateral Multi-Agent Hierarchy governed by Domain-Driven Design (DDD).

What is a Multi-Step DAG? A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a deterministic task pipeline where execution flows strictly forward from prerequisites to dependent outputs (Directed) with zero infinite loops (Acyclic). Independent balance sheet extractions run in parallel, while cross-table ratios wait for their exact upstream inputs before converging into the final decision policy.

The Specialist Advisor does not write paragraphs of text. Its sole responsibility is to evaluate available physical table rubrics against declarative banking covenants:

When the Generalist Crew Manager receives the LBO query, it feeds the extracted table headers to the Specialist, which compiles an ExecutionPlanDTO composed of 5 non-negotiable credit pillars:

Because each task has designated keywords and an explicit formula, the tasks execute sequentially or in parallel against our Physical Grounding Engine.

As established in Part 1, all tool calls are executed in Python using exact Decimal arithmetic.

In our Renault SAS 2024 benchmark test (LOGS_ECHANGE_GEN_SPEC_LBO_RENAULT.md), the runtime produces audited outputs anchored to exact physical lines:

The arithmetic outcome is definitive: 8.50 years of cash flow are required to extinguish existing debt. According to LboCovenantPolicyVO ($> 5.0\text{ years}$), an LBO without massive capital restructuring is strictly unfeasible.

Now comes the ultimate vulnerability: How do we guarantee the LLM does not distort this finding when writing the final executive briefing?

Most agent frameworks rely on the LLM's own self-critique (e.g., "Review your previous response and fix any errors"). As research has repeatedly demonstrated, this triggers sycophancy and confirmation bias: the model rationalizes its mistakes rather than catching them.

What does GenRM stand for? GenRM stands for Generative Reward Model—an adversarial verifier pattern introduced in Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction (arXiv:2408.15240). While frameworks like NVIDIA's post-training pipeline for Nemotron-3.5-Bolt use GenRM at train time (RLHF/RLVR alignment), we apply the same generative verifier pattern at inference time inside a 2-Layer Hybrid Neuro-Symbolic GenRMCritic with absolute veto power before any memo reaches the C-suite.

To achieve true enterprise readiness without relying on fragile regexes alone—and without wasting GPU cycles on obvious arithmetic errors—we architected GenRMCritic as a two-stage neuro-symbolic gatekeeper:

Every percentage extracted from the draft memo must match a certified result in the FinancialRuntime registry within a $0.05\%$ margin. If the model hallucinates "an operating margin of 42.5%" when the certified runtime output was -18.47%, Layer 1 issues an immediate VETO with zero LLM calls.

The most insidious failure in financial AI is directional polarity inversion or strategic verdict contradiction expressed with unexpected phrasing.

Consider these real adversarial cases verified against live Nemotron 3.5 Bolt in our E2E benchmark:

Here is our production 2-layer GenRMCritic implementation (with an offline deterministic fallback when no GPU/model backend is injected):

When a VETO is issued, the Generalist Crew Manager initiates a single targeted correction turn, injecting the explicit rejection reason into the synthesizer's context.

When all gates clear, the engine outputs an auditable, executive-ready memorandum. Below is the actual verbatim output (synthese_complete) generated end-to-end by our live Nemotron 3.5 Bolt pipeline + Python IEEE-754 runtime + Hybrid Neuro-Symbolic GenRMCritic on Renault SAS's audited 2024 standalone accounts (comptes sociaux, elapsed_s: 104.08s, certified_count: 4, genrm_calls: 2, GenRM verdict: [PASS]):

(Note on the 2024 figures: On Renault SAS's standalone 2024 accounts, CAF rose +83.02% from €1,378M to €2,522M while Financial Debt fell -37.55% from €7,487M to €4,676M, bringing Debt/CAF down to 1.85x and Gearing to 55.2% — clearing LboCovenantPolicyVO thresholds as FAVORABLE, whereas earlier 2023 standalone debt levels of €10,587M vs. €1,245M CAF yielded 8.50x and UNFAVORABLE.)
